title: Boston Baked Beans
subtitle: Slow-cooked haricot beans in a molasses and mustard sauce
excerpt: Boston baked beans are haricot beans cooked very slowly in a sweet and sour sauce of molasses, mustard, and brown sugar. They're darker and richer than tinned baked beans and need several hours in the oven, but almost all of that time is completely unattended.
sourceNotes: Boston baked beans are one of the oldest American regional dishes, with roots in colonial New England. The molasses-and-mustard combination is the traditional Boston formula.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze in portions. Reheat from frozen in a covered pan with a splash of water over low heat.
recipe.batchNotes: Boston baked beans improve with reheating. Make a large pot and eat over several days.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Soak the beans overnight. Make the dish a day ahead: the flavour deepens significantly.

content.text: Boston baked beans are haricot beans slow-cooked in the oven in a sweet, sour, dark sauce of molasses, mustard, and brown sugar. They require a long time in the oven, around six hours, but almost no active work. The beans go in dry and come out deeply flavoured, with a thick, dark sauce and a soft but intact texture.

Soak the haricot beans overnight in plenty of cold water. Drain and rinse before using. Pre-soaking reduces the cooking time and ensures even cooking. Don't skip this step: dried beans go into the pot unsoaked and they'll be unevenly cooked after six hours.

items.prepNote: dried, soaked overnight in cold water, drained

content.text: Heat the oven to 140°C (fan 120°C / gas mark 1). In a heavy oven-safe pot (a Dutch oven or deep casserole), fry the {{smoked-bacon-lardons}} over medium heat until the fat renders and the bacon is lightly coloured. Add {{white-onion}} and {{garlic}} and cook for five minutes until softened.

Stir in {{molasses}}, {{dark-brown-sugar}}, {{english-mustard}}, {{cider-vinegar}}, {{worcestershire-sauce}}, {{ketchup}}, and {{sea-salt-fine}}. Add the drained {{haricot-beans}} and pour in {{stock-chicken}}. The liquid should just cover the beans. Bring to a gentle simmer on the hob, then cover and transfer to the oven.

Cook covered for four hours. Remove the lid and cook for a further two hours, checking occasionally, until the beans are completely tender and the sauce is thick and dark. Add a little water during cooking if the beans look at risk of drying out.

items.symptom: The beans are still hard after six hours
items.cause: Beans not soaked long enough, or old beans.
items.fix: Soak overnight for at least eight hours. Old beans (stored for more than a year) may never fully soften. Cover and return to the oven in 30-minute increments until done.

items.symptom: The sauce is too thin at the end
items.cause: Lid left on too long, or too much liquid added.
items.fix: Remove the lid for the final two hours to allow the liquid to reduce. The sauce should be thick and syrupy, not watery.

items.symptom: The beans are too sweet and one-dimensional
items.cause: Not enough acid to balance the molasses and sugar.
items.fix: Add another tablespoon of cider vinegar and taste again. The finished dish should be sweet, sour, and deeply savoury in balance.

items.symptom: The beans dried out and caught on the bottom
items.cause: Oven too hot, or insufficient liquid.
items.fix: Add 100 to 200 ml of water and stir. Reduce the oven temperature to 130°C. The beans should be submerged in liquid for the first four hours of cooking.

content.text: Boston baked beans are one of the oldest American regional dishes, with roots in colonial New England where molasses was the dominant sweetener imported from the Caribbean. The dish was traditionally cooked overnight in a brick oven, the low, sustained heat is the same principle as this recipe. The name 'Beantown' for Boston comes directly from this dish. Serve as a side with hot dogs, grilled sausages, or slow-cooked meats.
